ML-Driven PVT-Variation-Aware Leakage Estimation

Digital VLSI Design — course project report. Team: Saumya Vira, Anish Toshniwal, Shrenil Patel, Het Selarka. Technology: PTM 45 nm HP (metal gate / high-k), VDD = 1 V; test circuit: 3-bit carry-lookahead adder. Report generated 2026-11-15 from the project's result files by scripts/z3_build_report.py.

Abstract

Leakage current of CMOS logic under process, voltage and temperature (PVT) variation is estimated with machine learning instead of full SPICE simulation. Four transistor-level models (NMOS/PMOS, ON/OFF) predict all four terminal currents (Id, Ig, Is, Ib) from VDD, temperature, width, terminal voltages and five BSIM4 process parameters. They are built from 64,000 single-transistor SPICE simulations (40,000 in the specification distribution plus 24,000 targeted near-rail samples; 49,600 used for fitting) and composed hierarchically into gate models (INV, NAND2, NOR2, AND2, OR2) and into a 36-gate, 192-transistor 3-bit carry-lookahead adder. On an independent evaluation set (200 new PVT corners, all 128 input combinations of A, B and Cin) the hierarchical estimate of the full adder's leakage has a median error of 0.58 %, a 95th-percentile error of 2.25 % and a mean accuracy of 99.22 %; individual gates reach 98.93 % and transistors (spec distribution) 98.56 %. The 99 % mean-accuracy target is therefore met at circuit level but not at gate or transistor level.

1. Introduction and objectives

Static (leakage) power is a first-order design concern in nanometre CMOS, and it varies by orders of magnitude with temperature, supply voltage and manufacturing variation. Characterising it with SPICE at every corner and input state is expensive. The project builds a hierarchical ML estimator: (A) learn transistor terminal currents from SPICE, (B) predict gate leakage from those transistor models and validate against transistor-level gate SPICE for all 18 gate/input cases at 200 corners, (C) compose a larger circuit from the gate models and validate against full-circuit SPICE. The stated target is up to 99 % mean accuracy.

2. Assigned technology, VDD and test circuit

item value
Model file models/45nm_HP.pm (PTM 45 nm HP, BSIM4 level 54)
Nominal VDD 1 V (sampled 0.9–1.1 V)
Channel length L = 45 nm
Widths 45–360 nm (1–8 Lmin)
Test circuit 3-bit carry-lookahead adder (inputs A, B, Cin: all 128 combinations)

3. Setup: SPICE simulator and environment

ngspice 44.2 (console build ngspice_con.exe), batch mode, driven from Python 3.13.14 on Windows 11 (numpy 2.5.4, pandas 3.1.1, scikit-learn 1.9.1, LightGBM 4.7.0, PyTorch 2.8.0 CPU for the final training). Every netlist (transistor, gate, circuit) contains .options gmin=1e-18 abstol=1e-18 reltol=1e-6 vntol=1e-9; single-transistor netlists drive every terminal with its own voltage source. Results are read from ngspice ASCII raw files (full double precision), not from printed logs. Currents are positive into the device terminal (I = −i(V_source)). Process variation is written into a fresh model card per sample: altermod toxe was found not to recompute the oxide-dependent BSIM4 terms in ngspice 44.2 (errors up to ≈5×). Isolated non-converging circuits are retried with raised DC iteration limits (tolerances unchanged).

4. PVT sampling methodology

Per transistor sample, independently: VDD ~ U(±10%) drawn first; Vd, Vs ~ U(0, VDD); W ~ U(1–8 Lmin); T ~ U(-40, 125) °C; vth0, toxe, ndep, u0, xj ~ U(±10%) of the device's own nominal value. Vg/Vb follow the case: NMOS ON (VDD, 0), NMOS OFF (0, 0), PMOS ON (0, VDD), PMOS OFF (VDD, VDD). Sample k is drawn from default_rng([case_seed, k // 1000]), so every sample is reproducible on its own. Seeds: data 1001 (+100 per case), split 2002, training 3003, gate/circuit corners 4004 (independent evaluation corners 5005). A corner draws VDD, T, one NMOS and one separate PMOS set of the five parameters, shared by all devices of that type.

5. Data generation and quality checks

40,000 single-transistor simulations, 40,000 succeeded, 0 failed; regenerating from scratch reproduced the four CSVs byte-for-byte. Supplementary targeted samples (near-rail terminals, |Vds| from 1 nV) were generated later for training only (4,000 + 4,000 per ON case, 2,000 + 2,000 per OFF case; separate files). Kirchhoff check (sum of the four terminal currents):

Data-check findings: OFF current falls about one decade per 0.1·VDD of source offset (negative Vgs + body effect; figure below); every non-nominal-toxe sample triggers BSIM4's 'toxe ≠ toxp + dtox, dtox ignored' warning because the specification varies toxe only; OFF-state body current is a nearly constant ~1e-14 A drain-junction current (no junction area/perimeter in the netlists); OFF-state Id flows against Vds in 28–36 % of samples with |Vds| > 0.1 V because channel current and gate-to-drain tunnelling nearly cancel. Full report: reports/a1_data_quality_report.md.

6. ML model comparison, hyperparameters and selection

Split 70/15/15 per case (7,000 / 1,500 / 1,500) with a fixed seed; scalers fit on training data; tuning and selection on validation only; test sets evaluated once. Features: VDD, T (K), log₁₀W, Vd, Vs, Vds, |Vds|, Vgs, Vgd, Vbs, Vbd, source offset from its rail, the five process parameters relative to nominal (+ asinh(Vds/1 µV) from v2 on). Targets: all four currents jointly, transformed with asinh(I/1 fA) (a signed log that is smooth through zero). Error metric: |I_pred − I_SPICE| / max(|I_SPICE|, 1 fA).

Target-transform study (LightGBM, validation median relative error):

transform nmos_off nmos_on pmos_off pmos_on mean
sign+log10|I| 6.89 % 8.11 % 5.52 % 8.49 % 7.25 %
asinh(I/1e-15) 7.82 % 8.68 % 5.48 % 8.78 % 7.69 %
asinh(I/1e-18) 8.98 % 9.39 % 5.92 % 9.30 % 8.40 %
asinh(I/1e-12) 9.57 % 10.93 % 7.43 % 11.52 % 9.86 %
asinh(I/1e-09) 21.73 % 27.98 % 13.46 % 29.31 % 23.12 %
linear 33.26 % 34.71 % 15.10 % 33.79 % 29.21 %

Sign + log₁₀|I| scored slightly better but needs a separate sign classifier per terminal; asinh(I/1 fA) was chosen as the best transform that every algorithm can use within a single regression model.

The MLP (tanh, three hidden layers of 128) won every case by 3–5×: the currents are smooth exponential functions of the inputs that a smooth network represents well, while trees give piecewise-constant fits over 11 decades and polynomial ridge cannot follow the exponentials.

Model history and selection rationale. v1 (A2) used sklearn L-BFGS; v2 (A2b) added the signed-log Vds feature and targeted samples, fixing ON-state Id/Is near Vds = 0 (OFF models were switched to v2 by a disclosed amendment). The improvement phase found that every earlier fit had stopped at sklearn's 3,000-iteration cap with training error ≈ validation error (under-fitting):

nmos_off (128, 128, 128) 1e-05 3000 3000 4.78e-05
pmos_on (128, 128, 128) 1e-05 3000 3000 7.24e-05
pmos_off (192, 192, 192) 1e-07 3000 3000 6.63e-05

8. Gate-level SPICE and ML methodology

Static CMOS gates; AND2/OR2 = NAND2/NOR2 + inverter simulated as one netlist. Sizing (not specified by the PDF): equal-drive sizing, unit inverter Wn = 2Lmin, Wp = 4Lmin, series pairs 2×, all within the ML training range:

gate device type W (nm) drain gate node source body
INV mp PMOS 180 out a vdd vdd
INV mn NMOS 90 out a 0 0
NAND2 mpa PMOS 180 out a vdd vdd
NAND2 mpb PMOS 180 out b vdd vdd
NAND2 mna NMOS 180 out a x 0
NAND2 mnb NMOS 180 x b 0 0
NOR2 mpa PMOS 360 y a vdd vdd
NOR2 mpb PMOS 360 out b y vdd
NOR2 mna NMOS 90 out a 0 0
NOR2 mnb NMOS 90 out b 0 0
AND2 mpa PMOS 180 n1 a vdd vdd
AND2 mpb PMOS 180 n1 b vdd vdd
AND2 mna NMOS 180 n1 a x 0
AND2 mnb NMOS 180 x b 0 0
AND2 mpi PMOS 180 out n1 vdd vdd
AND2 mni NMOS 90 out n1 0 0
OR2 mpa PMOS 360 y a vdd vdd
OR2 mpb PMOS 360 n1 b y vdd
OR2 mna NMOS 90 n1 a 0 0
OR2 mnb NMOS 90 n1 b 0 0
OR2 mpi PMOS 180 out n1 vdd vdd
OR2 mni NMOS 90 out n1 0 0

200 corners × 18 cases = 3,600 SPICE runs (0 failed, 0 logic errors). Leakage definition: I_leak = Σ_k V_k·(−i(V_k)) / VDD over the VDD rail and the input sources (static power / VDD, includes gate tunnelling drawn from inputs held high). Every transistor terminal has a 0 V probe; Σ V·I over all terminals equals the source power to 1e-6.

ML gate prediction: each transistor's Vd, Vg, Vs, Vb come from its connections — inputs exactly 0/VDD, bodies on the rails, and internal/output node voltages (out, x, y, n1) taken from the gate SPICE runs, as the PDF permits; the gate predictions therefore depend on SPICE node voltages. The ON/OFF model is chosen by gate bias; the AND2/OR2 inverter gate (n1; median 4.6 µV, at most 0.32 mV from a rail) is snapped to the nearest rail. Leakage = Σ over transistors of (Vd−Vs)·Id + (Vg−Vs)·Ig + (Vb−Vs)·Ib, divided by VDD: identical to the SPICE definition by Tellegen's theorem, KCL-consistent per device, and insensitive to ON-channel currents at Vds ≈ 0. Fed with SPICE's own transistor currents this code reproduces the SPICE leakage of all 3,600 cases. Inference runs with subprocess execution blocked (no hidden SPICE).

Node-voltage record (spec §5): results/final/gate_predictions_partB.csv and ..._newcorners.csv list, for every gate record, the SPICE leakage, the ML leakage, the SPICE-measured node voltages (spice_node_out, spice_node_x / spice_node_y, spice_node_n1, as applicable) and the node voltages supplied to the transistor models (ml_input_node_*). The ML-input voltages are the SPICE reference voltages used as model inputs, as step 4 of the spec prescribes; they are not predicted by ML. They are read back from the actual model inputs and checked to be identical to the SPICE values for every record.

10. Larger circuit implementation

Gi = Ai·Bi, Pi = Ai ⊕ Bi, C1 = G0 + P0·C0, C2 = G1 + P1·G0 + P1·P0·C0, C3 = G2 + P2·G1 + P2·P1·G0 + P2·P1·P0·C0 (carry-out), Si = Pi ⊕ Ci. Every carry is computed directly from G/P (verified: no carry depends on another), multi-input terms are trees of 2-input gates, XOR = AND2(OR2, NAND2) with NAND2(Ai, Bi) shared with Gi = INV(·). 36 gates (15 AND2, 12 OR2, 6 NAND2, 3 INV), 192 transistors, identical sizing/bodies/model cards. All seven inputs (A2..A0, B2..B0, Cin) are driven at exactly 0 or VDD, so every input combination is 2⁷ = 128 vectors (vector_id = A + 8·B + 64·Cin); the Boolean model is verified exhaustively. The Cin = 0 half was simulated first; the Cin = 1 half was added later with the same netlist generator, corners and options (separate *_cin1 files). Full-circuit SPICE at the Part B corners: 25,600 runs, 0 failed; outputs equal A+B+Cin and all 36 internal nets are at their logic levels in every run. Gate list: data/circuit/cla3_gate_list.csv; netlist: netlists/circuit/CLA3.cir.

ML estimate: a Boolean simulation gives each gate's inputs; each gate's leakage is the gate model of §8 for that gate type / input pattern / corner (gate-internal voltages looked up from the isolated-gate SPICE references, i.e. SPICE-derived); the circuit leakage is the sum over the 36 gates. No full-circuit SPICE quantity is used.

Composition check (no ML): summing the isolated-gate SPICE leakages reproduces the full-circuit SPICE leakage with median error 0.0062 % (p95 0.046 %) at the Part B corners and 0.0068 % (p95 0.049 %) at the new corners. Loading between gates is negligible at leakage-level currents, so the circuit error is the transistor-ML error. It is smaller than the gate-level error (median 0.58 % vs 0.78 %) because the 36 per-gate errors partly cancel.

12. Detailed error analysis

12.1 Transistor level

Ig and Ib are the easiest terminals (median 0.16 %–0.47 %); Id/Is carry most error (median 0.67 %–1.16 %), worst for ON devices at small |Vds| and for OFF devices where the channel and gate-to-drain currents nearly cancel (zero crossings make relative errors unbounded). Sign accuracy 99.7 %–100.0 %. Optimisation was the dominant limit of the earlier models (iteration cap, under-fitting); after it was removed, coverage of the near-rail region became the limit, partly fixed with extra targeted data.

12.2 Gate level

Per-device attribution (final models, Part B corners, all 3,600 gate samples): for every transistor instance the device-power error |P_ML − P_SPICE| was computed against the SPICE transistor currents of the same gate run. OFF transistors account for 88.3% of the summed device-power error, and the device with the largest error is an OFF transistor in 85.4% of the gate samples; 89.4% of the OFF-device error comes from OFF devices with (nearly) the full supply across them (|Vds| ≥ 0.9·VDD). In the three least accurate cases the device that most often has the largest error is NOR2 11: mpb (pmos_off, W = 360 nm, 95% of corners); NOR2 10: mpa (pmos_off, W = 360 nm, 56% of corners); NOR2 01: mpb (pmos_off, W = 360 nm, 88% of corners).

12.3 SPICE reference integrity

One new-corner gate record (AND2 00, corner 83) had a spurious operating point: with rbodymod = 1 ngspice's default solve converged to a non-physical internal body-node state (1.07e-8 A instead of 5.28e-10 A). Re-solving every reference with gmin stepping from the start (SPICE only, no ML) flagged only this record:

set kind records flagged max_rel_diff
data/final_eval/gates gates 3600 1 1.93e+01
data/gates gates 3600 0 5.56e-06
data/final_eval/circuit CLA3 12800 0 1.07e-05
data/circuit CLA3 12800 0 9.15e-06
data/circuit_cin1 CLA3 12800 0 1.36e-05
data/final_eval/circuit_cin1 CLA3 12800 0 9.30e-06

It is corrected in a separate file (original kept); the corrected value is the solution whose transistors match isolated single-transistor SPICE.

13. Limitations and possible improvements

  • Mean accuracy on independent data: circuit 99.22 %, gates 98.93 %, transistors 98.56 %. The 99 % mean-accuracy target is therefore met at circuit level but not at gate or transistor level. Longer training (some fits still hit the iteration cap), larger seed ensembles and more near-rail data would likely help; each MLP fit costs 1–2 h of CPU on this machine.
  • Gate (and therefore circuit) prediction uses SPICE-recorded gate-internal node voltages, as the PDF allows; a fully SPICE-free flow would need a node-voltage model (e.g. solving KCL at internal nodes with the transistor models).
  • Specification-inherited model assumptions: only toxe varies (BSIM4 keeps toxp nominal); no junction area/perimeter (body leakage ~1e-14 A, not ∝ W); widths of the gates are an assumption (equal-drive sizing).
  • Relative error is ill-defined for currents crossing zero; tail statistics on near-rail data should be read with that in mind.
  • Non-unique SPICE operating points (internal body nodes) can corrupt references silently; the uniqueness check should be part of every reference generation.
  • Earlier test sets were reused across model versions (disclosed); the primary claims use data created for, and evaluated once in, the final phase.

14. Conclusion

A hierarchical, physics-aware ML flow estimates PVT-dependent leakage from transistor to circuit level. Fitted on 49,600 single-transistor SPICE samples (of 64,000 generated for model development; a further 20,000 were simulated only as held-out test sets), it predicts the 3-bit carry-lookahead adder's leakage on unseen PVT corners with 0.58 % median error and 99.22 % mean accuracy over all 128 input combinations, and individual gates with 98.93 %, with no SPICE run at prediction time (the gate-internal node voltages are taken from gate-level SPICE references, §8). The decisive factors were the signed-log target, power-based (Tellegen) gate accounting, fully converged network training, targeted data near the rails, and SPICE reference integrity checks. The 99 % mean-accuracy target is therefore met at circuit level but not at gate or transistor level.
